..Very little change versus 24 hours ago. The large 
scale pattern has a storm system moving across the northern tier of 
states and high pressure aloft centered over northern Mexico and the 
western Gulf. A trough starts to dig south along the Pacific Coast 
on Sunday, as Hurricane Polo moves northward off Mexico to west of 
the Baja tip. Monday into early Tuesday, an area of low pressure 
forms over central California within the deepening trough over 
California, as Polo starts to make an eastward curve into Gulf of 
California south of the Baja Spur. Tuesday into midday Wednesday, 
the upper low moves from west to east across central Arizona 
dragging a frontal boundary/trough axis across the state, with the 
remnants of Polo tracking northeast across central Sonora and 
northern Chihuahua.   

Dry conditions will continue through tonight across southeast 
Arizona. PWATS start to increase on Sunday as the trough begins to 
dig to our west and we start to tap moisture to our south/southwest. 
PWATs come up into the 1.0 to 1.3 inch range by late in the day 
Sunday. Much of this moisture increase will be in the mid/upper 
levels, resulting in significant mid and high clouds along with a 
slight chance of showers and thunderstorms Sunday afternoon and 
Sunday night.  

Monday and Monday night PWATs jump up into the 1.2 to 1.6 inch range 
as the trough deepens to our west and Hurricane Polo curves east 
across the southern Baja Peninsula, the Gulf of California and then 
makes landfall near Ciudad Obregon. The flow across southeast 
Arizona at this time will turn southerly tapping this deep moisture, 
as the upper low and associated trough begin to push in from the 
west. Precipitation chances increase across the forecast area during 
the day Monday into the 40-50 percent range across much of the area, 
with 70 percent POPs in the White Mountains. POPs then increase 
significantly Monday evening into Tuesday morning into the 65-85 
percent range across most of southeast Arizona, with 90+ percent 
POPs in the White Mountains.  

Tuesday into midday Wednesday, the upper low and trough axis will 
shift eastward across the state and precipitation chances will 
gradually wind down from west to east. Across western Pima County 
the precipitation chances are expected to end during the early 
evening hours Tuesday and then during the morning hours Wednesday 
across eastern portions of the forecast area. 

Behind the upper low and trough Wednesday afternoon/evening, there 
will be a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms along the New 
Mexico state line, with the rest of the forecast area remaining dry. 
High pressure aloft then builds over the eastern Pacific Ocean and 
southeast Arizona dries out significantly under westerly flow 
Thursday into next weekend.  

Given the deep moisture across southeast Arizona Monday and Tuesday 
and the strong dynamics associated with the upper low and frontal 
boundary/trough axis there will likely be isolated severe 
thunderstorms over this time frame, along with the potential for 
flash flooding. Low end probabilistic guidance (25%) for storm total 
rainfall shows around 0.50 inches in the Tucson metro, lesser 
amounts west of Tucson and values of 1.0-1.5 inches along the New 
Mexico state line. High end storm total probabilistic guidance (90%) 
shows 2-3 inch totals across much of southeast Arizona, with a 
pocket of 4+ inches in the Greenlee County. Our official forecast 
has 1.0-1.5 inches in valley locations from Sells eastward and 1.5-
2.0 inches in the mountains. WPC has all of southeast Arizona 
highlighted in a SLGT Risk of excessive rainfall Monday and the 
eastern half of southeast Arizona in a MDT Risk Tuesday. 

Given the synoptic setup and the potential for heavy rainfall/flash 
flooding, have elected to issued a Flash Flood Watch from 11 am 
Monday through 11 pm Tuesday. For more information on this product, 
please refer to PHXFFATWC. While this time frame incorporates most 
of the expected heavy rainfall across southeast Arizona, some main 
stem rivers may have significant rises past the ending time of this 
watch due to response times.  

High temperatures will be a couple of degrees above normal through 
Sunday, lowering to 4-9 degrees below normal Monday through 
Wednesday, before warming back up to near normal late next week.
